title: Garbage In, Garbage Out: Engineering Reliable AI Document Extraction Pipelines

LLM and then wonder why the results are so expensive, inconsistent, and full of hallucination. Our next speaker is here to show us how to fix this by
engineering reliable end-to-end extraction pipelines. Our next Our next speaker is a staff solution engineer at Apprise with over a decade of experience in solution engineering, digital

industry 4.0. He has a deep technical focus on OCR, SDK integrations, and workflow automation. Today, he is here to share some practical engineering patterns to help us build smarter, more
predictable document extraction pipelines. Please help me in inviting Nazir Sayed on stage. Please give him a big round of applause. >> [applause] >> Over

So this is the architecture that most of us have in mind. Scan the document, run the OCR and pass the text to LLM or any AI model and get the result.
And this is what we see in the market and I guess I have talked with more than 15 people here in the audience that have
the same model. It's really simple, three steps, it's really simple. It looks right and this is what every product demo shows. And with a clean digital PDF it might

to photograph with his camera to submit for him pension. Or a sick person with shaky hand is trying to capture a photo and submit it

agency and to other companies to be processed. So if you look at this OCR in the center, so let's go back one step. This is how
we actually work, but in reality, what happens at each of these stages? At the input level, you will get blurry, skewed skewed images. This is really hard word
to pronounce. Because the source is a phone camera, so you are photographing with your own phone camera. There are billions of them out there with bad cameras, bad
lighting. You don't have professional scanner. And in the middle, you have an OCR which will turn that image into large bunch of unstructured data,
without layout, without field, without meaning. And at the end, we will send entire block into cloud API or to your AI model. And this is really expensive process.
It's a privacy risk because you are sending sending the complete data into your AI. And the output become unpredictable because you are asking from your AI to
make sense of a mess. And notice none of these failures are the AI model's failure. It is just every step is try to push its problem to the
next phase. So, what actually happens in the reality? At the input, you will get blurry images because the source is a phone camera. All right, I guess we said this, but I
did not move these slides. So, these are the problems that we have with each of these steps. So, now if you look at the OCR in the
center, OCR actually have three problems within itself. It fails because of these three issues. First, you have the image quality. If your image quality is bad, your OCR
accuracy will will drop shortly. And nothing later in the pipeline can't fix that. You can't basically recover data that I've never been captured. And then you have the the complexity.
Your document might have tables, it might have images, stamps, multicolumn layout, and when you flatten all of this into wall of plain data, you
lose a structure that gives this document its meaning. And then you have context. So, OCR can be really successful, it can read the character, it will convert it
into into text the pixels into text, but the pipelines might still fails because it doesn't know the structure of the data, doesn't know the metadata behind the OCR, so it
does not understand if the number of your invoice is an invoice number, is a date, is a VAT number, is a sum, is a
quantity for one volume. So, the question is why does this matter? So, we can still run it and maybe AI can give us the result results.
So, it matters because of three reasons. First, you have the cost. Sending raw data as an OCR to LLM will carry thousands of unnecessary tokens.
And that will scale with your document volume. Remember millions of documents per day? And you would just multiply all of those with thousands of token per day.
And then you have the reliability. If the input is inconsistent, your output will be inconsistent. So, at the end you will put human in the loop anyway. So,
human has to review all of the information because you can't trust your AI results. So, you are losing money, you are losing time. And also is a privacy issue.
So, imagine all of those private information, your invoices, your contract, your health record, when you send the complete raw data to your AI, those are the private information that
you can't get back. Those are security risk and compliance issue, especially here in Europe under GDPR. So, for these three reason, we have to
fix this problem. And the fix will look like this. And you can notice here we are not talking about better, bigger AI model, better prompting.
The fix is a new pipeline with five different stages. And each stage has one distinct job. In the capture level, we check the image
quality on the device the moment that photo has been captured. In the processing, we try to process that image. We will crop it, we will
clean it, we will filter it, and we will score it before we send it to OCR. And now OCR can run on a clean image,
and we will show you in a demo how important that is. But OCR alone is not not enough because we are losing the structure. So, we will
extract the structural data. We will get the field, the table, the key volume pairs instead of block of text. And we will also provide the confident level.
Because if my extraction is not confident that this part of information is correct, we want to validate it by putting human in the loop.
So, now the output of this pipeline would have the data and the meaning and the metadata so AI can process it. And the principle here is really simple.
Each stage in the pipeline will make sure that data for the next stage can be processed by it. In the previous model, each stage would try to
push its problem to the next one, and then you will end up everything at the AI level. But here, the data that will leave the validation
and will be sent to your model are already fixed because we are trying to fix the problem in each stage individually. So, now let's look into the demo.
I will run this invoice, the one that I talked about at the beginning. I photographed this at the checkout. And we will run it through the both
pipeline, the naive one, the old one with three steps, and the new one. I will see the result, and we will look for three things. We will look for the
processing time, how much computation power do I need to process this invoice? We will look for accuracy, the error rate, how accurate my results are, and
also we will look for the shape of output, how readable, processable this output is for an AI model. And we'll look into both of the models
and compare them side by side. So, this is the first one. This is that photo that I have photographed and I made sure that is readable. So, when I
zoom in, I can still read everything. It's really big. It has a lot of noise in it. It's a raw photo and I'm running it
through Docling OCR without any correction, exactly the way that my camera captured it. And in reality, we are getting images which are much, much worse than this picture.
The first thing that I noticed after running this one through OCR that the processing time took 190 seconds. More than 3 minutes to process one
image. The size is really big. There is a lot of noise in it. And for that reason, I made a recording. We didn't want to sit here
for 3 minutes just to see result of one document. Now, multiply this by millions of document that you submit to your health insurance, your car insurance, to any
government agency for them to process and to get the data off. But that is not the only thing. We also look for the accuracy.
If you look here down there, it will show now the name of company. There are some mistakes. The P has been changed with an O.
In the software, F and T has been missed. So, software is I don't know what. And in Belgium, L and I been replaced. And whole structure is
not so nice. There are structural errors that are also errors in the recognition of the text. So, let's look at the first fix. How can
we make this OCR results a bit better? The first stage of the fix is to fix the input. So, what we do is we use the same photo
and I will run it through an SDK on my premises for the reason to automatically crop it to have perspective correction, to filter it and quality check, and do
scoring of this image before sending it to OCR. And here you can compare both of them side by side. I reduced the size from
almost 5 megabyte to 340 kilobyte. And that will speed up the process itself. I removed all of the shadow and I made it nicer.
And all of this process took milliseconds, but for sake of argument, let's say I spent 1 second processing this image. Remember I had 190 seconds
for that OCR. Now what we'll do is we will run this image into the same OCR model. So I will go to the DocLink.
I will not change anything with an OCR. I will just change the input. This time I am running the corrected image. And the first thing
that I noticed is the processing time dropped from 190 seconds into 77 seconds. So I have a 60% of reduction in processing time, and that is the money
that you save in your computational cost. And that's not all. With reduction of the time, the whole structure of the document on the outside is also really nice. You can
see it visually. A price is now correctly identified. Software has an F and T, and also Belgium now has an I instead of L. So you have better
accuracy with reduction of the time just by changing the input. Now imagine if any company will put this correction phase before sending docu- raw data to
an OCR. So now what we did is we made OCR faster. We made it more accurate just by providing better quality image to the
DocLink. But there's an important point. Every even perfect OCR has a built-in limitation. Its job is to turn pixels into characters, into text, and it stops
there. It gives you the character, not the meaning. So, the table structure, the field name, the relationship between volume, all of that is lost in the flood
text. The output that we see on the OCR level is just flood block of text. And the missing structure is exactly what your AI needs. The AI should
understand how this information are placed in the document. This structure that you see here is really important. Where they are located, of information are there,
what's the relationship between them. So, to fix this, we have to go one level up. We have to extract the structure JSON from the PDF.
Instead of raw text, we have to extract the fields, the tables, the volumes, the location where they are located. Because this information is readily
usable by LLM. And also, we love JSON. You can parse JSON, you can choose those important component and feed it to your AI, and you don't necessarily need all
of the private information, and some of the information are actually not necessary. You can skip all of them out. And this is what basically we see on
daily basis. I had this conversation with, I guess, more than 15 of you sitting here at this event. And this is what we see in the
last year, that companies and developers are moving from manual formatting and sending raw data or OCR to an AI to getting more structured JSON format.
Because what happens with an structure with an raw OCR is there are gap in understanding of the structure of document. And what LLM does the best is trying to
fill the gap by guessing. And that is where hallucination is coming from. It tried to guess what this one should look like. So, let's see how this JSON output will
look like. I have another video for you, and then we go to the live demo. Let me connect here as well. So, in this example, you will see I am using

the device. The alternative would be to have all of this and I have computational power on my server to process those emails. So now we have covered everything. We
talked through capture level and we went through the whole new pipeline. You can read these details from after and before. But if I just sum it up the journey that
we have taken together, we have started with a system that accepted any photo, send it to OCR, get block of data, unstructured data, and send the whole
thing into third-party app or to AI or LLM model, and will get me a result I cannot explain nor trust. So I'm losing money, I'm losing
accuracy, I'm losing time. And we ended up with a system where there were control and checks on every step, and then output would be structured JSON
with a metadata that I can parse, I can get the sensitive information out, and I can send it to an AI, and I can be sure
that my results are cheaper because I'm sending small intentional part of the information, and they are more accurate. And if you notice here, nowhere in the new
solution we are suggesting bigger AI. We are not talking about better prompting, get this model or the other model. All what we are saying is
if you give it better input, you will get better output. So the outcome, the number that matters, we increase the accuracy and the confident will go up because the cleaner
structure will give you fewer error. We have shown that with only OCR, how we improve the error rate. >> [cheering] >> And also the cost of token will go down
because you will send smaller intentional text instead of the whole whole data. So here with this new pipeline, you are basically saving time, money, and increasing accuracy. And in
engineering and development, that is really rare to have at the same time. But in this example, you can have them both at same time.
So, if you take one sentence home from this presentation, it would be that AI doesn't fails on documents, it fails on pipeline. So next time your extraction results are
bad, you don't need to reach out for bigger model, you don't need need to reach out for better prompting. All you need to do is to go backward and see how
this document has been processed, what kind of data I'm feeding to my AI. And if you improve that, your end result will be improved automatically.

than happy to look into it. Thank you, everyone. >> [applause] >> Thank you, Nazir. That was really insightful talk into how we can improve
